ANDY HAMMERLINDL AND RAFAEL POTRIE

15. ANALYSING THE FLOW

In section 13, we constructed a continuous vector field X on the closed surface S. Since in this setting ges is in ideal position, its vertical sublamination A cs projects via n : M — S to a geodesic lamination A c S. Together, X and A have the following properties:

(1) the vector field X is tangent to the geodesic lamination A; (2) the vector field is zero at a point p if and only if n (p) is a center circle and we refer to these as the critical points; (3) each critical point lies on an isolated geodesic in A and we call these geodesics the critical geodesics; (4) each critical geodesic contains exactly one critical point; (5) at each critical point, the index of X at p is in {-1,0, + 1}; moreover, if we consider a small disk D centered at p and split D along the critical geodesic to produce two half-disks, then the index of X at p is in {½, 0, ½} on each of the half-disks.

Item (3) is given by lemma 9.1 and item (5) by lemma 13.1. The plan now is to first excise the non-isolated leaves of A from S, producing a surface with boundary So c S where A n So consists only of isolated geodesic arcs, each of which is compact. We then split So into a number of "regions" R; by cutting along the "critical arcs." By applying the Poincaré-Hopf theorem to the vector field X restricted to a region Ri, we show that at least one of these regions has positive Euler characteristic and therefore must be a topological disk. Its pre-image n' (Ri) must contain half of a vertical leaf of cu, and this causes a contradiction, completing the overall proof. For simplicity, we assume that the continuous vector field X integrates to a flow o on S and we explain in the following remark how to adapt the proof when this is not the case.

Remark. The definition of a dumbbell and the proof of proposition 14.1 do not actually rely on X integrating to a flow & on all of S. We can instead define an outflow edge o as having a small neighborhood U such that any integral curve starting at a point x € U and tangent to X must remain in U until it hits o. The proof of proposition 14.1 only considers the flow + on the lamination I. In our setting, I will be a geodesic lamination and so the flow is well defined. After applying the proposition and restricting to a subset So c S, we may replace X by a smooth approximation such that X is unchanged on the finitely many arcs of An So which contain critical points. Thus, we may freely assume that X integrates to a flow o.

Let I be the sublamination of A consisting of all of the non-isolated leaves in A. Apply proposition 14.1 to I and let So denote the subset S\ int (K) given by the proposition. Each boundary component of So is therefore a dumbbell.
